name: Marco Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a corrugated-box die-cutting line at a packaging factory. My two-year technical diploma got me through the machine drawings, but the knack is hearing when a dull die begins tearing a fold. I set the feed, check the cut, and stop the press if a guard is loose. A neat box coming off the belt can still fail when somebody folds it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit around home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia works reception at a dental practice, and our two children are still at school. We have a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved; my pay is ordinary for this work, even though I lead the shift. A couple of other plants are close enough to commute to, though I would have to see their actual openings and shifts. I sometimes ask an AI tool to simplify a parts manual, then check the part number against the machine plate. I trust a new method after an operator has shown it working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that quieter AI leaves our box press much as it is. The order sheets may move faster, but somebody must still check a scored fold and a guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia and I can meet the mortgage on our present wages. Four months saved is useful for a setback, and a slow change gives me time to keep the younger cutters up to standard. I would rather have a reliable line than a new gadget every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press checks and show the apprentice how to test a fold after the die warms up. From each newly paid Saturday shift, I would move a set amount into the family savings account after the mortgage and food are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled. I know what my wage buys and which part of the press needs a real pair of eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does an apprentice first make a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They look at the cut face and forget to fold the box. A score can be a millimetre out and still look tidy on the belt. I make apprentices fold samples before they adjust the die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using that AI manual tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For plain explanations, now and then. I check the drawing number and the lockout instruction in the actual manual before anyone works on the press. The AI answer does not sign my safety sheet.

say: I would **tell** the crew a faster order sheet cannot test a scored box.
I would **show** apprentices how to fold samples before changing a die.
think: Our **two** wages meet the mortgage and four months saved gives us room.
The **present** press role remains useful in a slow AI picture.
do: **Keep** checking the die-cutting press and teaching fold tests.
**Transfer** new Saturday-shift pay into savings after mortgage and food.
feel: **Settled** with predictable wages and familiar safety checks.
S0.quote: I make apprentices fold samples before they adjust the die.
fieldNote: **Marco** leads a die-cutting line and uses occasional AI explanations only after checking actual machine documents.
The **household** has four months saved and can meet its mortgage on current wages.
He would **add** newly paid Saturday-shift income to savings, not merely move an existing reserve.

steps.text: Keep checking press guards and finished box folds
Transfer new Saturday wages to savings after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that better office software arrives before any robot takes a stack of boxes from our press. I want management to show us which duties and hours it proposes to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The die and guards still need attention, but a robot stacker could eventually take the packing hands and let management combine shifts. My own lead hours might be cut when orders dip. Four months saved will not make a smaller wage comfortable for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a guarded stacker demonstration on our press and compare the damaged boxes with our usual count. I would use the AI manual tool for part descriptions, not operate the stacker from a screen. If the factory posts a paid lead role after that change, I would apply only if its wage covers the mortgage and its hours let me collect the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the roster, even though I am curious to see a working machine. I need a written press shift plan before I can call it an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would let you try the stacker controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proven guard, paid supervised practice and the fitter beside me for lockout. Watching a demonstration would not teach me the controls. I would ask for a real training slot before accepting responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no lead opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check posted die-cutting jobs at the other nearby plants while I still have my present wage. A vacancy has to exist and its pay and school hours have to work before I apply. I will not resign because someone says work is probably available.

say: I would **ask** management for written hours before robot stacking changes the roster.
The **office** software change comes before physical box handling changes.
think: My **press** skill still matters, but a later stacker could cut lead hours.
**Four** months saved cannot replace a lasting reduction in my wage.
do: **Request** a guarded stacker demonstration and compare damaged boxes.
**Apply** for a posted lead role only with mortgage-covering pay and school-compatible hours.
**Check** nearby posted die-cutting work if the plant offers no suitable opening.
feel: **Anxious** about possible roster cuts, curious only after safe proof.
S1.quote: I need a written press shift plan before I can call it an opportunity.
fieldNote: **Marco** requests a demonstration; he does not claim to have operated or trained on a robot stacker.
A **new** lead application needs a posted paid role, enough wage for the mortgage and school-compatible hours.
If **no** suitable role appears at his plant, he separately checks posted local die-cutting jobs against pay and hours.

steps.text: Request guarded stacker demonstration and compare damaged boxes
Apply for posted plant lead role only with mortgage-covering pay and school hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AGI handling orders in 2028 is one problem; capable robots stacking, setting and clearing presses around 2031 are another. We need the factory to state its staffing plan while we still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our machine shifts to disappear once robots can change the die and clear the jams. My lead job at the die-cutting press may buy me a little time, but it does not pay a mortgage after the line goes dark. Four months saved would go fast, and I would lie awake counting the payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia and I would cut the planned kitchen refit and write down the mortgage, food and school costs this week. I would ask the factory for written redeployment and severance terms. I would apply for a posted local maintenance-assistant job only if it offers paid supervised safety training, enough wage for our bills and hours that fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I could still make calls and complete forms, but I would not confuse that with a secure income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your diploma take you straight into maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me drawings and electrical basics, not a licence to reach into a robot cell. A supervisor would have to offer paid safe instruction and check me on isolation first. I would not take the job without that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the savings to start a box business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months is our family buffer, not the capital for a factory. We would hold it for bills and first find out what paid work is actually posted. The kitchen refit can wait.

say: I would **separate** 2028 order software from capable press robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for staffing and redeployment terms while wages still arrive.
think: I **expect** major machine-shift loss by 2031 despite being a lead.
**Four** months saved could vanish quickly against a mortgage and two children.
do: **Cancel** the kitchen refit and list household bills.
**Ask** the factory for written redeployment and severance terms.
**Apply** for posted local maintenance-assistant work only with paid safe instruction, bill-covering pay and school hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless over mortgage payments.
S2.quote: My lead job at the die-cutting press may buy me a little time, but it does not pay a mortgage after the line goes dark.
fieldNote: **Marco** expects a large cut to machine shifts only after capable robots arrive about three years after AGI.
His **maintenance** application requires an actual posting, paid supervised safety instruction, sufficient wages and school-compatible hours.
The **family** cancels a planned refit and preserves four months of cash for bills rather than treating it as business capital.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen refit and list mortgage food and school costs
Ask factory for written redeployment and severance terms
Apply for posted maintenance-assistant job only with paid safe training bill-covering wage and school hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is time for a proper machine-maintenance course, if the plant offers a place and pays people while they learn. AGI changes order work in 2031; capable robot work comes around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 when those robots can work the press. My diploma and years setting dies would help, but I need actual robot isolation practice before I could maintain one. I have a mortgage and cannot swap a wage for an unfunded certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for the plant’s recognised maintenance course if it offers a funded place, paid hours around school pickup, and supervised guard and lockout practice. After completing it, I would apply separately for a posted local maintenance job only if the salary and shift cover our bills. If the course place never comes, I would keep working the press and look at posted nearby operator jobs with enough pay and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously anxious about the eventual line change. Five years helps me only if a real paid place and a real job follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an online robot course be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I could read it for vocabulary, but reading does not prove that an arm is isolated. I need a fitter to watch me stop and test the cell on paid time. That is the part worth training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the maintenance wage is lower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set it beside the mortgage and school costs before I apply. If the posted wage falls short, I would stay on the press while searching other local work. A robot maintenance certificate by itself does not fill the mortgage gap.

say: I would **ask** for a funded paid maintenance place with supervised robot isolation.
**AGI** changes orders in 2031 before hands-on robots around 2034.
think: At 51, the **diploma** is a start but not robot safety competence.
An **unpaid** course or lower wage would strain the mortgage.
do: **Apply** for an offered funded paid course only with supervised lockout and school hours.
**After** course completion, apply for posted maintenance work only if wage and shift cover bills.
If **no** course place, search posted local operator jobs with sufficient pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about eventual work loss, guardedly open to proven paid training.
S3.quote: A robot maintenance certificate by itself does not fill the mortgage gap.
fieldNote: **Marco** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded maintenance place with paid school-compatible hours and supervised practical safety work.
**After** training, a separate application depends on an actual local vacancy, sufficient salary and a workable shift.
**Without** a course place he keeps his present press wage while checking posted local operator jobs.

steps.text: Enrol in offered funded paid maintenance course with supervised lockout and school hours
Apply after completion for posted maintenance job only with bill-covering salary and shift
Search posted nearby operator jobs if no course place and pay and hours work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew ten years lets us teach the next cutters and test a safer maintenance route before robots work the press. I want the training wage and the future job written down, not promised across a tea break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 when thinking AI changes the orders and 56 around 2039 when capable robots can handle the machinery. Our children will be older, but the mortgage may still be there. A long warning gives me time to move, provided the paid route is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the line and, if offered a funded paid maintenance course with supervised robot safety practice and workable hours, I would take it. Once qualified, I would apply for a posted nearby maintenance job only if its pay covers our bills and its shift works for home. If the course is not offered, I would seek posted operator work at a wage and shift we can live on. I would put new Saturday-shift earnings into savings after ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about losing the trade I know, but I can picture a practical route. I would be more settled after seeing the course terms and a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the apprentice learn first over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to stop the press when a guard moves, and how to fold a sample box before turning the die screw. I would teach those habits even if a robot stacks the finished run. Speed without a sound box is just waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a new maintenance offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A vague job title, a shift that leaves the children stranded, or a wage that cannot meet the mortgage. I can learn a new robot press control, but I cannot learn away the household bills. I would ask to see the posted duties and pay.

say: I would **ask** for a written paid training route and posted maintenance work.
**Experienced** cutters should teach guard and fold checks before robots arrive.
think: At 53 in 2036, I **may** still lead the line while order tasks change.
At 56 **near** 2039, I need paid work if robots take the hands-on press duties.
do: **Keep** leading the press while checking an offered funded paid safe course.
**After** qualifying, apply for posted bill-covering maintenance work; without a course, seek posted operator work with sufficient wages and hours.
**Save** new Saturday wages after ordinary bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual wages, more hopeful with a concrete paid route.
S4.quote: I can learn a new robot press control, but I cannot learn away the household bills.
fieldNote: **Marco** favours training that preserves a wage and checks robot isolation through supervised practice.
A **later** maintenance application requires a posted local job, sufficient pay and workable home hours.
An **operator** search is a separate fallback if no course is offered.
He would **add** new Saturday earnings to savings while ordinary household bills are met.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots could remove our press shifts around 2031 and four months saved would not carry the mortgage for long. A funded paid safety course and a posted local job with a bill-covering wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: My children see a box, not a die cutter. I want them to know that a simple box takes skill and a safe machine. A neat box coming off the belt can still fail when somebody folds it.

headlineQuote: A neat box coming off the belt can still fail when somebody folds it.
portrait: **Marco** Farah, 43, leads a corrugated-box die-cutting line and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He **shares** a mortgage and two school-age children with dental receptionist partner Nadia, with typical pay and four months saved.
He **uses** AI now and then to explain a parts manual, then verifies numbers and lockout instructions against the machine documents.
His **practical** traditional outlook accepts proven technology and paid apprenticeship while he teaches guard and fold checks.
**Possible** robot shift cuts worry him; rapid expected loss keeps him awake, while paid training and posted work offer a route.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could erase most die-cutting shifts and exhaust four months of household savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised maintenance training and posted bill-covering local jobs with workable school hours.
